Additionally, there was a burgeoning sense of nationalism among intellectuals and reformists who sought to modernize China and address the humiliation of colonial domination. Answer_with_full_information: The question of why China, during the early 20th century, did not pursue a colonization strategy akin to Japan’s is indeed fascinating and multi-faceted. Firstly, we must consider China’s historical context. This fragmentation made it extraordinarily challenging for China to project power outward. In stark contrast, Japan was undergoing a rapid modernization and industrialization process following the Meiji Restoration, which not only stabilized its internal governance but also equipped it with the military and technological means to assert itself on a global stage. Additionally, while Japan sought to prove its worth and secure resources through imperial expansion — often justified through an ideology of superiority — China’s political discourse was fraught with a strong sense of nationalism and resistance to imperialism. Chinese leaders and intellectuals were increasingly concerned about sovereignty and self-determination, perhaps leading to an ethical stance against the very practices that were victimizing them. It’s a poignant irony; instead of following Japan's imperial path, many in China were focused on reclaiming dignity and unity. Thus, rather than an ethical aversion to colonization per se, it was China’s compromised state, internal struggles, and a burgeoning national identity that shaped its response to the imperialist wave sweeping across the region.

Old_Answer: Who, me? My VN friends couldn’t pronounce any of my other names, so they named me Tài Lộc 財祿, which is a good name. We were only about a hundred meters from the border with NVN, so it was dangerous. Every night before we went to sleep, our leaders told us to remember which way was south; to put our important documents in our pockets, not under our pillows; and at the least sign of danger, run south without stopping to ask. We were close enough to see the muzzle flashes from NVN artillery. We visited the cemetery where 2,000 refugees were buried. They had been slaughtered by communist forces in 1972. It was quite a time. Quảng Trị, summer 1974, photo by me. There were still a lot of unexploded shells, so we had to be careful where we went. When we finished, we visited Hué, and spent a night on a small boat on the Perfume River. The next morning I visited the Palace, which was still in ruins from 1968.
